I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

The authors developed a useful tool for analysis of ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN and CUT&TAG data. The work was carefully done, the tool is well described.

Importantly,  we tested the Rocketchip  tool and it works well. We plan to use it going forward. As such others in the filed will also find it useful.

The vast repositories of multi-omics sequencing datasets continue to grow at an impressive pace. Yet, these datasets remain relatively underutilized, as the development of computational tools has lagged behind the rapid expansion of multi-omics data. The present work is carefully executed, and the Rocketchip tool is clearly described and reasonably well validated. My lab tested Rocketchip on one of our own ChIP-seq datasets and obtained results comparable to our traditional workflow, while saving time. Thus, others in the field are also likely to find it useful.

Although the authors list several limitations, I suggest adding the following points for consideration:

1.
                Reproducibility and applicability across data types – Demonstrate that Rocketchip can be used reproducibly and replicably for other bulk multi-omics sequencing data types, such as RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and DNA methylation sequencing.

2. 
                Cross-method performance comparison – Provide a side-by-side comparison of Rocketchip’s performance when analyzing ChIP-seq vs. CUT&RUN and/or ChIP-seq vs. CUT&Tag datasets generated from the same samples (e.g., Daly A, et al., 2024 [Ref 1]).

Reviewer Expertise:

Multi-omics of disease.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

In this protocol by Haghani et al, the authors developed an automated bioinformatics workflow, named Rocketchip, which analyses local ChIP-seq data or ChIP-seq data from NCBI and SRA. Overall, this protocol is well written and the GitHub repository is well documented. I only have a few minor concerns:

Correct me if I am mistaken: In the section: Use cases

Conducting -> ChIP-seq data analysis via all software combinations, my impression is that Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) is more often used to map the transcriptome data to the genome rather than ChIP-seq data. I am not sure whether it is reasonable to use or mention this aligner here, which might be somewhat misleading. Especially the authors did find that 'When STAR was used as the aligner with CisGenome, peak counts were the lowest'.

Although I do appreciate the efforts that the authors made to evaluate the number/efficiency of peak counts for all software combinations, yet I wonder whether the authors have compared the differences between those identified peaks: are most of them overlapping or each algorithm is able to identify their unique peaks.

Lastly, I am curious about the ability and performance of identifying weak-signal peaks, on top of the F1, precision, and sensitivity scores of this platform, given that the binding strength of chromatin associated proteins and histone modification abundances have large variation across the whole genome.

Are the conclusions about the tool and its performance adequately supported by the findings presented in the article?

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This is a useful report on the international clinical trials landscape with a focus on regulatory oversight and number of trials conducted in relation to socio-economic status of countries. Unsurprisingly lower income countries appear to have less regulatory oversight and overall very few registered clinical trials and of these a lower proportion of academically led trials compared to North American and Europe.  The report also points out limitations of clinical trial registration data in particular the difficulties obtaining information on ongoing or completed trials in the lower income countries.  Some comments:

- authors should provide a bit more detail about WJHA 75.8 as the current description is a bit vague and generic.  What are the key gaps to be addressed?

- authors should acknowledge that establishing clinical trials as a useful method to test new treatments strategies has been academically led, and industry has adopted these methods as they are well accepted for evaluating evidence and for promoting their products.

- Clinical trials activity, both non-commercial and commercial, depends on the strength and depth of academic trials leadership and the extent of collaboration with national and international clinical networks. Many non-commercial and commercial trials rely on international networks of investigators in different income countries but as the report rightly suggests the presence of these trial in low income countries is relatively low.

- the aim of complete clinical trial registration and reporting is well established and if this is not happening in lower income areas then the issue is likely related to local governance, resources and academic capacity to address these issues.

- I think the Actionable Recommendations about descriptive data to help ensure greater equity about trials are all very sensible but appear to be telling us what we already know and should be doing. It i likely that obtaining more complete data on trials activity globally will confirm what is presented in this report.

- The main issue appears to be the lack of trials and trials reporting in low income countries where the burden of disease is highest. This article should focus much more on these specific issues and how to address them.  One useful method is for experienced centres in higher income countries to be funded by WHO or other non commercial emtities to partner with academic centres in lower income countries to develop clinical trial expertise and capacity.  This could boost clinical trial activity and quality in lower and lower-middle income countries through training schemes and exchange of knowledge which in turn will help to train the next generation of researchers and trialists.

- I was not sure how useful figure 3 was for example the profile for Africa and Americas looked quite similar but we assume the number and composition of the trials would be quite different.

This manuscript discusses limitations in our understanding of the global clinical trials landscape, and makes a series of recommendations to address these.  It addresses an important topic, but could be improved through several modifications.

1. The work is based on a scoping review, but there are no details on the methods or sources used.  There is a link, however this does not provide information beyond the specific database to which the link is directed.  An understanding of sources would be valuable.

2.  The definitions used to define sponsorship are unclear.

3.  In Figure 3, the categories are unclear.  What is meant by education, by healthcare.

4. In the recommendations, more focus could be placed on establishing and curating durable sources for information on clinical trials.  Given that trials are the foundation of medical knowledge, a mechanism - an archive, a library, or something analogous - would be important, and seems an important step beyond merely registering what one is doing.  Additionally harmonizing registries would be an important advance, if we are unable to settly on a single global registry.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

Thank you for your manuscript titled “Case Report: Duodenal duplication: A case report of a rare gastrointestinal anomaly”.

The authors describe a case of a 14-year-old boy with duodenal duplication and its treatment strategy. While duodenal duplication is a relative rare condition, numerous reports have been published on the treatment and diagnosis of this disease.

I would like to ask the authors: What is the novel point of this study compared to previous reports?  Because this is a case report, unless this is the first case ever reported worldwide, you need to identify and state some unique aspects or contributions of this case that differentiate it from existing literature. Without such novelty, this report risks being viewed as repetitive and may fail to capture readers’ interest.

Minor comments

CT and MRI images appear very similar. I recommend adding sagittal and/or coronal views to better illustrate the lesion’s position and size.

In figure 4, I cannot understand the anatomical structures. Please provide annotations to help readers understand the anatomy.

In figure 5, it appears that this image might be rotated with the left side positioned upward (based on the liver position). If so, please correct the image orientation.

Reviewer Expertise:

My areas of research are Statistics, Data Science, and Business Management. I have extensive experience conducting Systematic Literature Reciew (SLR), Bibliometric as well as research using Big Data approaches. This background allows me to thoroughly asses the methodoligal rigor, data science application, and theoretical contributions of this article, especially in the context of employee performance research and bibliometric mapping within business and management statistics.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

1. The article sets a clear context, establishing why a detailed examination of employee performance research is essential. Authors clearly stated its vital relevance by anchoring the analysis in the unprecedented post-pandemic transformation of work. Further the study highlights that existing performance paradigms need to revisted, post pandemic justifying a timely bibliometric mapping to uncover the new research priorities and thematic clusters shaping the future of employee performance. The objectives of the review are then presented in a precise manner, and clearly stated why the contribution is significant.

2. This study presents a clear methodological framework for bibliometric analysis. The authors clearly mentioned the Scopus as the data source and the time frame (2020–2025), ensuring transparency and ease of replication. PRISMA 2020 guidelines used in this study adds to the rigor and objectivity of article selection, while the adoption of Bibliometrix (R) and VOSviewer further adds credibility to the analysis as they are the leading tools in this research. The outlined approach, from performance evaluation to PRISMA, exclusion of articles, identifying research trends, detecting key themes/topics, grouping contemporary themes, identification of the most influential publications in employee performance research, normalized citation provides a logical and well-structured roadmap. Overall, the methodology is robust, systematic, and sufficiently detailed to serve as a reliable model for future research.

3. The statistical analysis adopted is well-suited to bibliometric study. The integration of Bibliometrix R for performance analytics and trend visualization with VOSviewer for co-word analysis and bibliographic coupling reflects a standard approach. The seven dominant thematic clusters, normalized citation analysis enhances validity by controlling for temporal and disciplinary biases. This combination ensures a robust synthesis of the intellectual structure and emerging trajectories in employee performance research.

4. The conclusions are firmly rooted in the empirical results. The seven thematic clusters identified through network mapping, alongside trend and citation analyses, provide direct and compelling evidence for the stated claims about the field's intellectual structure and evolution.

5. Key Deficits for Living Systematic Review (LSR) Classification:

Title: The absence of the term "Living Systematic Review" or a clear variant. The specific time-period end date (2025) further states that it is not a living, review.

Absence of a Defined Search Update Schedule:  The publicly stated schedule for periodic updates is missing. Frequency: How often will the search be repeated (e.g., monthly, quarterly, biannually)?

Update Triggers: What criteria will trigger an update (e.g., a volume of new publications, emergence of a landmark study)?

Stopping Criteria: Under what conditions would the "living" status be suspended or ended?

Absence of Justification for a Living Approach

No Protocol for Integrating New Evidence: There is no mention of the operational processes for managing updates like:

How new records will be screened and integrated into the existing analysis. How the bibliometric maps (clusters, networks, trends) will be revised and re-interpreted.

How version control will be managed and previous iterations archived.

Conclusion and Recommendation:

In its present form, this study is a well-executed  bibliometric review with a defined endpoint. To be transformed to an LSR framework, the authors must:

Amend the title to include "Living Systematic Review."

Present a detailed protocol outlining the update schedule, justification, and methods for evidence integration by securing a commitment for the long-term resources. Without these critical components, labeling it as a Living Systematic Review would be inappropriate.

However, the current title is apt for the article and need not be transformed to LSR framework.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

This submission provides a rigorous theoretical analysis; the proofs appear correct and the assumptions are clearly stated. My main concern is reproducibility: no code is provided and several hyperparameters are unreported. The related-work coverage is adequate. Overall the significance for the broader community seems modest.

This article attempts to expand Bourdieu's notion of cultural capital to fit the field of public health and epidemiology. In doing so, it takes a purely theory-based approach, basing the findings on prior research on the link between culture and health.

While I appreciate the attempt to clarify how cultural capital should (can) be applied to research related to health, I do not think the authors succeed in doing so in this article.

My main concern is how 
                culture and 
                cultural capital seem to be used by the authors rather interchangeably. Their definitions often seem to go beyond cultural capital, in which the 
                capital part of cultural capital seems to be forgotten: many of the suggestions the authors 'expand' the concept beyond its usage as something that can be 'exchanged'. Drawing from anthropological research, they argue that exchangeability is not necessary for cultural capital, but I am not convinced by their argumentation here.

A second main concern is two-fold. First, I am not convinced by the 'novelty' of the idea of a form of cultural capital that can be applied better to health and well-being. On the one hand, this is because I am of the opinion that the 'original' cultural capital is applicable enough for this (see amongst others the work of Thomas Abel and Joost Oude Groeniger), and on the other hand, similar attempts have been (successfully) made in the past already (see, e.g., Shim (2010)'s work on 
                cultural health capital).

Second, the article does not make a convincing case for how this new form would work in practice. Many of the newly proposed concepts, like 
                existential cultural capital and the three domains of relationship discussed in Table 3 remain vague and hardly applicable. As such, I do not see the added value this article has to the (admittedly limited) body of research on cultural capital and health.

Some smaller issues:

- At various times, the authors allude to cultural capital as an 'individual factor', at some point going so far as to suggest a contextual form is needed (challenge 3). While I can see how it can be defined as an individual factor (e.g., when it's operationalized in statistical models), this conceptualization seems to overlook how cultural capital is based on societal structures of how 'dominant culture' is defined.

- Methodologically, the article is a bit unclear. It's a theoretical paper based on previous literature, yet it is far to incomplete to be considered a (systematic) literature review. Even if the authors' goal was not to paint a complete picture of the field, some core research of the cultural capital and health field is missing (e.g., abovementioned Abel, Shim, Oude Groeniger). Also more recent work about cultural capital itself could benefit the theoretical depth (e.g., Van der Waal et al., 2024).

- There are some (commendable) remarks about equality and equal chances for all (e.g. Japanese tea ceremonies, "legally guaranteed existential cultural capital" (p. 7), or "a healthy society that leaves no one behind" (p. 11). I would argue that research on cultural capital 
                exactly shows this is not the case. It shows that there is some (cultural) hierarchy in place in most societies that goes beyond e.g. economical inequalities. As such, I do not understand the attempt to create a form of cultural capital that is equal for all.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

First, many of the dimensions listed above—such as statistical analysis—are not applicable to this conceptual paper.

The article aims to link a particular conceptual model, informed by Bourdieu’s perspective on cultural capital, to the field of epidemiology. The authors argue that this framework may enhance our understanding of epidemiological processes. Certainly--the use of cultural capital is relevant and has found its way into social epidemiology (e.g--Abel, T. (2008) [Reference 1]) The authors reference previous work by Wieiss and the Explanatory Model Interview Catalogue, which emphasizes subjective and culturally specific understandings of health and illness and recognizes  that specific "symptoms" have culturally specific meanings. As such, they may or may not be related to clinical syndromes depending upon their culturally specific meaning. The psychiatric anthropologists come on Arthur Kleinman also makes this case through his field research in mainland China. (See, for example,  Ware, N. C., & Kleinman, A. (1992) [Reference 2])

The methodology of the current  paper is described as a theory-driven literature review. The authors highlight key distinctions between Bourdieu's approaches and public health paradigms, particularly with regard to social epidemiology.

In their discussion of five central challenges in applying Bordieu's model to epidemiology, the authors provide illustrative examples for the first two challenges. However, for challenges three through five, while providing  examples drawn from cultural and religious traditions (e.g., Buddhism and Christianity) are included, the article would benefit from more direct applications to public health. and /or illustrations from cultural epidemiology The lack of concrete public health examples weakens the integration of the conceptual model with epidemiological practice.

In the conclusion, the authors suggest that their model could foster a shared language for conducting culturally informed research in public health. However, due to the limited number of practical examples and the insufficient demonstration of integration with public health frameworks, the article does not present a compelling case for adoption by epidemiologists and public health professionals.

As such, this paper represents a potentially useful beginning of a conceptual dialogue which will hopefully be expanded upon.

I have reviewed the submission and confirm that I have the necessary expertise to evaluate its scientific merit. This study addresses a crucial and relevant topic: the awareness of occupational hazards among dental professionals, including both final-year students and practicing dentists. The research is valuable as it highlights specific knowledge gaps and misconceptions that have direct implications for the health, safety, and well-being of dental practitioners. The finding of no significant difference in awareness between students and experienced dentists is particularly noteworthy and warrants further discussion.

While the study is promising, there are several key areas that require significant revision to strengthen the methodology, deepen the analysis, and enhance the overall impact of the manuscript. The following report provides a summary of the article's findings and expands on four major points that must be addressed before the article can be considered scientifically sound for publication.

1. Inability to Determine the Study's Response Rate

A significant methodological limitation is the inability to calculate the study's response rate. The authors report that 198 dental professionals participated in the survey. However, they also state that the precise number of eligible individuals who were invited but declined to participate or were absent could not be determined. Consequently, the response rate could not be calculated. This omission raises concerns regarding potential non-response bias, as the resulting sample may not be fully representative of the target population of dentists and final-year students in the selected hospitals. It is plausible that individuals with a higher pre-existing awareness of occupational hazards were more inclined to participate, potentially skewing the results toward a higher overall awareness level.

2. Discrepancy in Awareness of Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs)

The results present a notable discrepancy regarding awareness of MSDs. Participants demonstrated high general awareness that MSDs are a common hazard in dentistry, with 85.9% correctly identifying them as such. In stark contrast, awareness of carpal tunnel syndrome as a specific and common type of MSD was exceptionally low, with only 14% of participants providing the correct answer. The manuscript's discussion section does not sufficiently explore the reasons for this significant gap between general knowledge and specific knowledge. An in-depth analysis of potential causes, such as deficiencies within the dental education curriculum regarding specific ergonomic-related conditions, would provide valuable context for this finding.

3. Substantiation of "Correct" Answers Regarding Mercury Carcinogenicity

The study classifies the belief that mercury in dental amalgam is a risk factor for oral cancer as incorrect. A majority of respondents (62.1%) held this belief. Given that a significant proportion of the professional sample holds this view, the manuscript's argument would be strengthened by substantiating the "correct" answer with a citation from an authoritative body, such as the World Health Organization or a major international dental association. This would provide a firm evidentiary basis for labeling the belief as a misconception and would offer readers important context.

4. Interpretation of No Significant Difference Between Students and Dentists

The finding that there was no statistically significant difference in awareness levels between final-year students and practicing dentists (p=0.575) is a key result that invites deeper interpretation. The authors propose this may be due to the large number of students in the sample or the adequacy of the formal curriculum. However, the discussion should also consider an alternative interpretation: the lack of difference could indicate a stagnation of knowledge among practicing dentists post-graduation, possibly due to insufficient or ineffective continuing professional education in occupational health and safety. Exploring this possibility would lend greater weight to the study's conclusion that continuous training is essential for enhancing and maintaining awareness among dental practitioners.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

1. Summary of article: The article analyzes how older adults become victims of tech-support fraud by reviewing 16 cases extracted from the AARP Fraud Tracking Map (2021–2024). Using qualitative coding in MAXQDA, the authors identify common patterns such as pop-up alerts, impersonation of legitimate support services, emotional manipulation, and barriers to reporting. The study highlights key vulnerability factors among the elderly and emphasizes the need for improved awareness and prevention strategies.

2. Abstract: Currently reads more like a background summary than a scientific synopsis. It should explicitly state the data source used (cybercrime reports, hotline logs, etc.; the methodological approach (thematic pattern analysis); and the main contributions to the field.

3. Literature review: The authors cite a wide range of relevant and fairly current studies, which shows good effort in gathering related literature. To strengthen the manuscript further, the literature review could integrate these sources more tightly into a coherent conceptual narrative and clarify how prior work informs the present study. Overall, I rate this aspect as “Partly,” with the suggestion to deepen the literature synthesis rather than expand the references list.

4. References: Although the manuscript lists 29 references, only references 1 through 16 appear to be meaningfully cited in the text or incorporated into the discussion. The remaining references do not seem to be engaged with, integrated, or mentioned in the body of the paper. The authors should integrate references 17–29 into the discussion if they are relevant.

5. Methodology: The manuscript describes conducting a literature search using Google Scholar as a methodological step. However, a narrative literature search is a standard component of all research papers and does not constitute a methodological contribution unless this article intends to be a systematic review, meta-analysis or scoping review, which it is not. Furthermore, reliance solely on Google Scholar limits the comprehensiveness and credibility of the literature review. The authors should justify their choice of sources and, ideally, include additional scholarly databases (e.g., Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO) to ensure adequate coverage. The current approach risks omitting relevant peer-reviewed work and may introduce search bias. Since the research design appears to be qualitative case analysis of AARP fraud cases, the authors should explicitly state the qualitative method employed, provide analytic procedures, and define how themes were derived. A clearer methodological framework is needed for transparency and replicability.

6. Findings: Findings are mostly descriptive. The manuscript would benefit from a deeper analysis on why seniors fall for specific scam mechanisms; linking findings to psychological/cognitive ageing literature, relevant theory and international reports; and clearly labelled tables/figures that show frequency distributions or patterns. Lack of analytical depth reduces the distinctiveness of the contribution.

7. Academic writing style: Several paragraphs contain only one or two sentences, which limits the depth of explanation and makes the discussion feel fragmented. In academic articles, paragraphs typically develop a clear idea supported by evidence, reasoning, or examples. I encourage the authors to expand these shorter paragraphs so that key concepts, findings, and interpretations are explained more fully to improve the overall coherence and scholarly tone of the paper.
